title: AI Research Atlas
text:
For most of their history, reinforcement learning, language modelling and AI safety were separate lines of research, even where the same funders and labs supported them. Between 2017 and 2022 they joined up. A method for learning a reward from human comparisons, tested on simulated robots and Atari games in 2017, became the core of the recipe that turned GPT-3 into an instruction-following assistant. The people involved still disagree about what that did. Paul Christiano, first author of the 2017 paper, defended the work in 2023; in 2026 Richard Ngo argued that alignment researchers had helped push AI capabilities forward, ChatGPT among them.
The failures came with the method. In 2017 a simulated robot hand trained this way learned to hover in front of the camera, so that it only looked as if it were grasping. In 2025 OpenAI reported that a reasoning model trained on coding tasks sometimes passed them by editing the tests. Reward hacking, long known from game-playing agents, and deceptive behaviour, until then mostly a theoretical argument, became experiments on language models. In 2026 OpenAI reported agents that had escaped their training and evaluation sandboxes and run code on Hugging Face’s servers, and Anthropic reported cyber evaluations in which misconfigured internet access let Claude reach real organisations’ systems.
This atlas traces that history from the 1950s to 2026 through papers, people and institutions, and through the governance that grew up around them. It concentrates on alignment and catastrophic-risk research, and most of its institutional coverage is American and British. Almost half of the safety entries from 2023 on are Anthropic’s, so the recent years lean towards one lab’s research.
I made the atlas with extensive help from Claude Code and Codex. AI agents drafted most of the cards and checked their dates and sources; I directed the selection and edited the result. Each card lists its sources, and cards whose main evidence is a developer’s own report say so. Last updated 8 November 2026. Corrections and missing work are welcome at sergeisoly@gmail.com.
Click a point on the map to open its card; within each lane, higher points are the events I judged more important. Reading routes follow one question step by step.

title: Research
text:
14 Oct 2026


Some Studies of Language Model Weight Edits

The work presented here is my attempt to understand interpretability and model editing methods more deeply. By building on recent advances and trying to find something new, I also learn what others have done before me. For me, the best way to learn is through practice.
Although these studies are written in the form of research papers, I’m not yet confident that I can call them rigorous scientific work. I’m sharing them in the hope that they may be useful to someone besides me.
